title: Slated Version - Around the Air Force: Recruiter Healthcare, Better EOD Robots, Ejection Seat Testing
description: This week's look around the Air Force highlights an effort to provide better healthcare solutions for recruiters in remote locations, an upgrade to explosive ordnance disposal robots, and testing of a new ejection seat configuration for the new T-7A trainer aircraft.
keywords: Around the Air Force, recruiter health care, better EOD robots, Ejection seat testing

transcript.text: Leaders from the Air Force recruiting
service . Defense Health Agency and
Tricare are collaborating to brainstorm
health care solutions for military
recruiters in remote locations . The
recruiting service is working to
identify locations with the greatest
challenges to medical provider access
to enable the defense health agency to
focus on areas where improvements are
needed . Most the trilateral
partnership also aims to educate
recruiters and their families about
health care options by engaging with
members prior to their first assignment
and developing a monthly briefing about
plans and benefits . The Air Force
Research Laboratory is leading the
development of a new system to enhance
precision for explosive ordinance
disposal . Robots in partnership with
the Air and Space Force tech connect
service . The new technology aims to
improve precision and safety for EOD
personnel by increasing depth detection
while controlling robots during counter
improvised explosive device operations ,
current rely on two dimensional cameras
to determine depth . The upgraded
system utilizes infrared sensors and
led lights to better mitigate risk in a
three dimensional environment .
Technical sergeant , Daniel Trombone
99th civil engineer squadron EO D team
leader says precision is everything for
an EOD technician because there's no
room for error . He adds , it's
critical for technicians to solve as
many problems as possible with their
robots before directly exposing
themselves to danger . A new ejection
seat configuration is undergoing
testing on the air force's newest
trainer aircraft . The T seven A Red
Hawk . The tests aim to ensure the
effectiveness of a drogue chute during
slower speed . Ejections , drogue
chutes are traditionally used to slow
the seat and occupant down at ejection
speeds above 250 knots . But before the
personnel parachute is deployed , the T
seven A program is collecting data in
dynamic environments with constantly
changing air speeds to provide proof of
theory and update modeling software for
ejection seat performance for a wider
range of pilots . That's your look
around the air force . I'm technical
sergeant Britt Crowley .
